occurrences.passage: \textbf{C3.} We show how peak-limit rankings change with the historical reference and breach assessment in these observed forecasting tasks. We compare same-history and shorter-history rolling controls across three windows with previously examined outcomes, using established score diagrams and error-weight preferences. For the distinct long-horizon legacy comparison, the preferred report reverses at a penalty ratio of about 20.6:1. Where the endpoint lineage evaluates intervals and Ehm et al. (2016) develop general score comparisons, we connect these diagnostics to monitoring limits with completed path labels. Sections~\ref{sec:evaluation}--\ref{sec:implications} support a four-part checklist: use matured labels, separate history and model changes, report scores with breaches, and check stability across periods and related series.

Quantile estimation and evaluation supply established tools for comparing conditional peak forecasts against historical rules on a shared response. Regression quantiles target asymmetric forecast errors, providing the basic statistical building block for the proposed conditional reports \citep{koenker1978}. Conditional autoregressive quantiles and quantile forests offer additional conditioning structures for forecasting applications that differ in response, predictors and estimation \citep{engle2004,meinshausen2006}. Learning-curve research documents diverse and sometimes nonmonotone relationships between training size and predictive performance across methods and data conditions \citep{viering2023}. Our fixed-period curves compare relative loss against a historical reference that also changes with training history, differing from an independent-sample expected-risk curve. Consistent scoring tools explain ranking differences across evaluation questions \citep{gneiting2011,ehm2016}; Table~\ref{tab:literature} locates the shared peak target, mature labels and matched reference design.

The inclusion of the issue position matters because a feasible peak limit must already cover the exposure observed at the forecast origin. Figure~\ref{fig:example} shows a real window selected by a fixed chronological rule, with an endpoint inside the limit and an earlier peak outside it. A successful endpoint interval can therefore answer a different risk question from a successful report for the full sampled peak. We evaluate the latter through pinball loss and count a breach precisely when the observed peak strictly exceeds the reported limit. This report monitors sampled net inventory; its known floor neither measures settlement cash needs nor establishes an optimal operating limit.

The experiment uses 32 independent repetition streams with common innovations across conditions and 72 evaluation issues per repetition.
